set.body:
Ranked #3 by the vignette reviewer, ABOVE the vocabulary problem, on the grounds that it blocks the reader even after everything else is fixed. I had not filed it and it deserves its own bead.

Searchlights are identified as [1,] through [6,] in introduction.Rmd:110-116. Nothing says row 2 is the searchlight centred on feature2. Edges are identified as edge_000001 through edge_000004 in evidence-pairing.Rmd:124, and the ONLY code mapping edge ids to node names sits in the hidden check chunk at :134-138.

The hands-on reviewer hit the same wall from the other direction and called it a papercut twice: rdm() values carry NULL rownames with the ROI labels living in a separate index element, and connectivity() values - which the README prints as the payload - are labelled edge_000001..4 with no from/to, so you must join against the edge index to know which row is seed to target.

THE LARGER VERSION OF THE SAME PROBLEM: nothing in 1263 lines of user-facing documentation says anything of the form 'region X shows a stronger identity effect than region Y'. There is not one finding in either vignette. Every example ends on a table of numbers with no claim attached.

That is why this ranks where it does. A reader can be given a shipped generator, a retitled section, a glossary, and a citation to G, and still arrive at a table of unlabelled numbers with no model of what a good result looks like.

Note this is NOT the same as bd-01KZY901ZPM73SBFAY79WR5PM7. There I verified that rdm() prints columns labelled 'face - house' and that the print methods are good. That is true, and it is the top-level view. The failure here is one level down: the MEASUREMENT axis - which searchlight, which ROI, which edge - is unlabelled everywhere, and the docs never interpret any of it.

FIX: label the measurement index in the printed views wherever the frame knows the labels, and end at least one vignette section on an actual claim about the data rather than on a table.
set.title: The reader never learns what an output row or column is, and never sees a finding
